description: EMAI Voyagers: a university group building a game where players design, launch and fly their own space mission, juggling budget, mass, power and communications trade-offs. Our team is already complete, so this page is for our members to join officially.
summary:
Everyone has watched a rocket launch, but few see what happens behind the scenes: the research, planning and building before liftoff, or what the spacecraft does after it leaves Earth. Moonshot shows exactly that.

In Moonshot, you design and fly a Moon mission in your browser. Your goal is the Lunar Ice Mapper: a 6U CubeSat that hunts for water ice in south polar craters that never see sunlight.

You build it in seven steps: planning, instruments, spacecraft, orbit, launch, communications and a go/no-go review. Each step changes the others. Add an instrument and it draws more power, so the solar array grows, the craft gets heavier and needs more fuel. Nine checks show where the design stands, and each failing one names the step that fixes it.

Then you fly the launch as a timing game: ignition, gravity turn, Max Q, staging and orbit insertion, each explaining what really happens on a real rocket.

In orbit you fly the mapping pass over real craters like Shackleton and Cabeus. Only an instrument that sees into permanent shadow finds the ice.

The mission then runs month by month and can stop on failures like a clogged thruster or a lost signal. A final report traces every missed requirement back to the decision behind it.

Every number comes from a real source: NASA’s CubeSat 101 for parts and costs, Lunar IceCube and Lunar Flashlight for instruments and failures, and LRO and GMAT for orbits and delta-v.
details:
Moonshot: the part of the rocket launch nobody shows you

Almost everyone has watched a rocket launch video, and it never stops being amazing. But the video ends right when the real story gets going. You don't see the years of research, the arguments over mass and money, the hundred small trade-offs that decided what went on board. And once the rocket clears the atmosphere, the camera cuts away and nobody sees what happens next.

Moonshot is the game about everything the video leaves out. Our goal is to teach people how a space mission really works, and to get them excited about the behind-the-scenes work, not only the launch.

YOU RUN THE WHOLE MISSION

You're in charge of a small space agency flying one mission, the Lunar Ice Mapper: a 6U CubeSat sent to find water ice in the Moon's permanently shadowed south polar craters. You pick the instruments, build the spacecraft, choose the orbit and the ride, and set up the link home. Then you stand in front of the go/no-go review and find out whether you got it right.

PREPARATION AND TRADE-OFFS

Every choice costs you something. Add an instrument and it draws more power, so you need a bigger solar array. That makes the craft heavier, so it needs more fuel to be captured into lunar orbit, and the budget tightens. Mass, power, budget, delta-v, data and time all push against each other, which is what real mission designers deal with every day. If something is wrong, the game says what it is and which step fixes it.

THE LAUNCH, FROM THE INSIDE

Launch Day is the moment people already love, but here you fly it: ignition, the gravity turn, Max Q, staging, fairing release and deploy. You feel why each step matters.

LIFE AFTER THE ATMOSPHERE

This is the part nobody shows. After launch your craft flies on, month by month, and meets problems taken from real missions: a build delay, a lost signal after deployment, a clogged thruster, a radiation reset, a ground station outage, a long eclipse, a detector that ages. Each one is a decision with a cost. When it reaches the Moon, you map the ice yourself in the Ice Mapper, sweeping the scanner over named craters like Shackleton, Cabeus, Faustini and Haworth. Your instrument and battery decide what you can see, and only an instrument that can see into permanent shadow finds anything there.

YOU FIND OUT WHY, NOT JUST THAT YOU FAILED

The starting design is modelled on Lunar IceCube. It flies, but its infrared spectrometer can't see into the shadowed craters, so it comes home almost empty-handed. Working out why is the first lesson, and the game never tells you the answer. The final report traces every miss back to the choice and the event behind it.
